sentences.text: Briefly stated, the facts as narrated in the FIR and charge- sheet are that on 19.05.2017 at about 07:00 PM, the deceased namely Shaloo Singh Chuahan (deceased) met with an accident and died, while she was travelling in car bearing Registration No. UP- 16DT-2533.
She has left behind her mother and her younger brother Shivam Singh as the dependents.
3. In response to the notice of petition, both the respondents appeared and filed their replies/ written statements.

3(i). In the written statement filed by the respondent no.1/Driver-cum-owner namely Sunil Kumar, he stated that he is not liable to pay any amount of compensation, as the vehicle of the answering respondents was duly insured at the time of alleged accident and the liability, if any, the insurance company is liable to pay the same.
His vehicle was insured with United India Insurance Company Ltd., at the time of accident.
Respondent No. 2/United of India Insurance Company has filed its separate written statement and stated that claim is not maintainable against the respondents.
It is submitted that there was no rash and negligent driving on the part of the Respondent No. 1 while driving the car No. UP-16DT-2533 on 19.05.2017.

It is further submitted that Petitioner No. 1 Smt. Neelam had intimated the SHO of Police Station Sec. 20 Noida, U.P. vide her letter dated 08.06.2017 that her daughter died on 20.05.2017 on account of the injuries sustained by her, while travelling in the car no.
_____________________________________________________________ MACP No. 113/17 ; Neelam & Ors. Vs. Sunil & Ors. Page 2 of 19  UP-16DT-2533, which overturned due to disbalancing at the speed breaker.

It has been further mentioned in the said letter that the aforesaid incident had taken place only by chance and there was no allegation of rash and negligent driving on the part of the driver of the aforesaid car.
It is also submitted that petitioners have not filed any document alongwith her claim petition which attributes any rash and negligent driving on the part of the Respondent No. 1.

Since there was no negligence on the part of the Respondent No. 1,
Respondent No. 2 Insurance Company has no vicarious liability to indemnify the Respondent No. 1, who is also the owner/insured of the aforesaid car.
Other general defences have been taken by Insurance Company.

ISSUE NO.1 8.

It is pertinent to mention here that as per settled proposition of law, in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani &
Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation &
Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303.

13. In view of the finding on issue no.1, petitioners are entitled to get compensation, however, the quantum of compensation still needs to be adjudicated.

COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION 14. Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claims Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance

A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).

15. The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D.
Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.

The relevant extract is as under:
 "Broadly speaking while fixing an amount  of compensation payable to a victim of an  accident, the damages have to be assessed  separately as pecuniary damages and  special damages.

Pecuniary damages are  those which the victim has actually  incurred and which is capable of being  calculated in terms of money-, whereas  non-pecuniary damages are those which  are incapable of being assessed by  arithmetical calculations.

In order to  appreciate two concepts pecuniary  damages may, include expenses incurred  by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii)
 loss of earning of profit upto the date of  trial; (iii) other material loss.
So far non-  pecuniary damages are concerned

, they  may include (i) damages for mental and  physical shock, pain suffering, already _____________________________________________________________ MACP No. 113/17 ; Neelam & Ors. Vs. Sunil & Ors. Page 10 of 19  suffered or likely to be suffered in future;
 (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of  amenities of life which may include a  variety of matters i.e. on account of injury  the claimant may not be able to walk, run  or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of  expectation of life, i.e. on account of injury  the normal longevity of the person  concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience,
 discomfort, disappointment, hardship,

sentences.text:
The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:
 4.

The provisions of the Motor  Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short)
 makes it clear that the award must be just,
 which means that compensation should, to  the extent possible, fully and adequately  restore the claimant to the position prior to  the accident.
The object of awarding  damages is to make good the loss suffered  as a result of wrong done as far as money  can do so, in a fair, reasonable and  equitable manner.

The court or the  Tribunal shall have to assess the damages  objectively and exclude from  consideration any speculation or fancy,
 though some conjecture with reference to  the nature of disability and its  consequences, is inevitable.
A person is  not only to be compensated for the  physical injury, but also for the loss which  he suffered as a result of such injury.

This  means that he is to be compensated for his  inability to lead a full life, his inability to  enjoy those normal amenities which he  would have enjoyed but for the injuries,
 and his inability to earn as much as he  used to earn or could have earned.

5. The heads under which compensation is  awarded in personal injury cases are the  following:
 Pecuniary Damages (special damages)
 (i) Expenses relating to treatment,
 hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
 nourishing food and miscellaneous  expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains)
 which the injured would have made had he  not been injured, comprising:
 (a) Loss of earning during the  period of treatment.
 (b) Loss of future earnings on  account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.

In routine personal injury cases, compensation  will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii), (a)
 and (iv).

It is only in serious cases of injury,

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is pertinent to mention here that as per settled proposition of law, in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani &
Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation &
Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303.
9.
The offending vehicle was registered in the name of R1.
It is not the plea of respondents that accident took place due to involvement of any other vehicle.
In such a situation, where R1 met with an accident on road resulting in his vehicle turning over, it was clearly a case of res ipsa loquitor and only R1 could explain how he was not responsible for the accident.
No such plea has been taken by R1 that his vehicle had some latent mechanical defect resulting in the accident.
In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Cmpany Ltd vs Smt.
Kamlesh and Others2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.
11. Thus, in view of the above, this Tribunal is of the opinion that petitioners have been able to prove that there is sufficient material on record to establish that the accident had occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by respondent no.1 and that resulted into grievous injuries to the deceased victim Shalu Singh Chauhan.
Therefore, issue no.1 is decided in favour of petitioners.
Insurance Company has not any evidence to show that the insurance policy was breached by R1/driver-cum-owner and no RE was led by R2/Insurer in this regard.
13. In view of the finding on issue no.1, petitioners are entitled to get compensation, however, the quantum of compensation still needs to be adjudicated.
COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION 14. Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claims Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance
A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).
15. The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D.
Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.
16. In Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.
The provisions of the Motor  Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short)
 makes it clear that the award must be just,
 which means that compensation should, to  the extent possible, fully and adequately  restore the claimant to the position prior to  the accident.
The object of awarding  damages is to make good the loss suffered  as a result of wrong done as far as money  can do so, in a fair, reasonable and  equitable manner.
The court or the  Tribunal shall have to assess the damages  objectively and exclude from  consideration any speculation or fancy,
 though some conjecture with reference to  the nature of disability and its  consequences, is inevitable.
A person is  not only to be compensated for the  physical injury, but also for the loss which  he suffered as a result of such injury.
Accordingly, the multiplier of 18 which is applicable to age group between 21-25 years shall be applicable in this case.
The established  income means the income minus the tax  component."
21. Since the deceased Shalu Kumar Chauhan was under the age of 40 years, prospects to the tune of 40% shall be added to his income in view of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of National Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Pranay Sethi and Ors.
After choosing the age, multiplier and income of the deceased, necessary deductions have to be made out of the income of the deceased towards her personal expenses.
